newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Catastrophes cost insurers 22 pct less in 1996.
newsitem.headline: Catastrophes cost insurers 22 pct less in 1996.

text.p: Global insurance losses from natural and man-made disasters fell 22 percent last year but were still high enough to continue a string of record claim years since 1989, Swiss Reinsurance said.
Catastrophes caused $12.3 billion of insured losses in 1996, out of a total of $50 billion including damage not backed by insurers, according to the latest issue of Swiss Re's Sigma research report.
"The past year may therefore be regarded as a continuation of the record series experienced since 1989, with total claims in excess of $12 billion," Sigma said in its edition 3/1997.
"Within this record series, however, 1996 did show the lowest claim level, as losses from natural catastrophes were relatively low," it added.

Natural disasters accounted for the larger share of damage with $7.9 billion, including the year's largest single loss of $1.6 billion from hurricane Fran in the southeast United States last September.
"Once again a billion-dollar loss was therefore recorded in the reporting year as in all years since 1989," Sigma wrote.
The most devestating natural catastrophes happened in Asia, including two periods of Chinese flooding that killed 2,700 people, but produced few claims due to a low level of insurance.
Storms and freezing weather in the United States produced 11 of last year's 20 most costly insurance losses from disasters.
"The U.S. therefore accounted for 64 percent of global insured losses," Sigma said.

Man-made disasters accounted for $4.4 billion in losses, led by five serious cases totaling two billion -- fires at Credit Lyonnais headquarters, the Channel tunnel and Duesseldorf airport as well as two bomb attacks in Manchester and London.
Sigma said overall insured losses were down 22 percent from 1995 when adjusted for inflation and U.S. dollar rates but did not provide a comparative figure.
The 1996 claims bill was 38 percent higher than the annual average since 1970, when Sigma started collecting the data.
Sigma's report on 1996 covered 341 catastrophes that claimed a total of 22,000 lives.
It said Asia was a high risk region with 50 percent of all 1996 catastrophes and 70 percent of resulting fatalities. But low insurance levels meant Asia only acounted for one-tenth of world losses.
"The reverse situation applies to the U.S./Europe, with its high degree of insurance: insured losses are high, despite a lower exposure to catastrophes," Sigma wrote.

The number of disasters overall had risen continuouslsy since 1970 due in part to more detailed information but also to higher population density, broader coverage for assets and a concentration of assets in industrialised nations, Sigma wrote.
"It is impossible to prove whether climatic change affects the number or the scale of natural catastrophes on the basis of Sigma data," the report said.
But it said the insurance industry must still at least consider the possibility of higher claims burdens in its scenarios for the future.
